prize_parts.citation: for discoveries of the physiology of GLP-1 and the identification of its active form, which enabled incretin-based therapies for type 2 diabetes and obesity

statement.case_for: GLP-1 physiology is the one candidate on which all six openings converge (five first places, one second). It offers a rare unbroken line from gut-hormone physiology and proglucagon processing to therapies with large, independently confirmed outcome trials in diabetes, obesity, cardiovascular and renal disease. The discovery is clear, original and mature, and the timing is strong. I still favour a physiology-centred trio of Drucker, Holst and Mojsov, because the prize rewards the discovery and its demonstrated change to the field rather than the engineering of a specific drug. That choice leaves out the industrial developer, which is a real cost I acknowledge below.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is attribution. Four names are credited and only three can be honoured. Mojsov's role in identifying the active truncated peptide is contested in the literature, and I have not verified the priority record. Excluding Knudsen can be read as ignoring the translation that actually delivered the clinical benefit, while including her shifts the prize toward drug development. Either choice has a defensible critique. A narrower concern is that a prize for the therapy class could appear to be crowding out candidates with a purer mechanistic discovery.

responses.point: Svenningsson proposes Drucker, Holst and Knudsen, treating the long-acting analogue design as the link from basic biology to therapy, and regards Mojsov's credit as a problem.
responses.response: This is the serious disagreement on the table, and I take it seriously. Knudsen's liraglutide and semaglutide work is why patients benefit at scale. But the Nobel question is the discovery, and the active-peptide step is part of the discovery chain, whereas analogue design builds on a discovery already made. A prize built around Knudsen would read as recognition of a drug programme at one company. I would revisit if the committee concludes that Mojsov's priority cannot be defended, in which case Knudsen is the natural third name. I am not persuaded that the uncertainty alone justifies dropping her.

responses.point: Sandberg ranks the unfolded protein response first, on conceptual originality, a mechanistically complete pathway and decades of independent confirmation, and puts GLP-1 second mainly because of the credit structure.
responses.response: I agree the UPR work of Walter and Mori is conceptually clean, with a tidy two-person attribution that GLP-1 lacks. I ranked it lower because its medical impact is still largely conceptual, with little clinical translation. For a medicine prize I weigh that difference. But I accept this is a judgement and not a fact. Sandberg's case that the cleanest attribution deserves weight is strong, and I keep UPR as a serious alternative if the committee cannot settle GLP-1 credit. I do not think a messy attribution lowers the merit of the discovery itself.

responses.point: Wahren-Herlenius ranks anti-TNF therapy second on the strength of the cytokine-targeting paradigm in chronic inflammatory disease, and ranks CAR-T third.
responses.response: Anti-TNF is clearly mature, but the paradigm is now widely used and the Feldmann and Maini credit leaves out important antibody and cytokine contributors. I did not rank it in my top eight, and I remain unconvinced it exceeds CAR-T on originality. I do agree with her that CAR-T is a plausible second choice. The weakness there is not merit but attribution, since Eshhar's early chimeric receptor concept is outside the credited names. That is why I keep CAR-T as an alternative and not as a co-prize.

responses.point: Perlmann ranks BCL-2 third, as a bridge from basic cell-death biology to venetoclax, and supports the Drucker, Holst and Mojsov configuration with GLP-1 timing described as arguably overdue.
responses.response: I agree with the GLP-1 configuration and with the judgement that timing is not premature. On BCL-2 I am less convinced, because apoptosis has already been recognised in 2002 and the Cory and Adams, Vaux and Strasser credits, with Tsujimoto uncredited, are messy. I do not rule it out, but it is not among my alternatives.

uncertainties: Whether Mojsov's priority for the active GLP-1 peptide is secure enough to carry a laureate place, or whether Knudsen should take that slot.
Whether the committee wants a physiology-centred prize or one that includes drug development, which decides the Knudsen question.
Whether a two-part prize pairing GLP-1 with a second distinct achievement is better than a single GLP-1 prize, given the three-person limit.
I rely on recollection of the historical priority record and have not verified it from the supplied evidence.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from the provided profile for the preferred B043 configuration or the alternatives B019 and B032. My co-authorship of the spatial transcriptomics paper and my single-cell and atlas work do not involve any shortlisted candidate's credited names. I would recuse myself from any item where a documented co-author or former trainee was credited.
